feedback: Correct full answer for the 2-teddy share: '6 each — it's fair because both teddies have the same number with none left over; I gave them out one at a time until they were gone.'
If a learner offers unequal piles and is untroubled by the difference, model one-for-you dealing, then count and compare both piles so equality becomes the test of fairness.
If a learner shares equally but never checks the piles match, prompt them to count both and confirm they are the same before calling it fair.
With an odd total (e.g. 13 between 2), name the leftover plainly rather than reteaching; noticing 'one left over, won't share evenly' is the goal, not resolving the remainder.
activities.intendedInsight: Fairness here means everyone gets an equal amount. When the total shares evenly there are none left over, and when it does not (e.g. 13 between 2), the leftover is simply named. A child shows understanding by checking the groups match, not just by giving everyone 'some'.
learnerActions: Share 12 counters fairly between 2 teddies so each gets the same. Say how many each teddy gets (6) and explain how you know it is fair.
Count each teddy's pile and compare — are they the same, with none left over?
Describe your method: 'I gave them out one at a time to each teddy until they were gone.'
Now share the same 12 counters among 3 teddies and say how many each gets (4); then answer the matching grouping question: how many groups of 3 can you make from 12? (4) — both are 12÷3.
Try 13 counters: can you still share them fairly between the 2 teddies? What happens? (6 each with 1 left over — it won't share evenly).
activities.title: Fair-share check with teddies

feedback: If a learner does not recognise a 'how many groups of 3?' problem as division, act it out with counters alongside a sharing version and name both as division.
If a learner thinks 12÷3 and 3÷12 are the same, show with counters that sharing 12 among 3 differs from sharing 3 among 12 — division is not commutative.
This sorting and matching can check whether the child holds both meanings; it checks classification rather than eliciting the physical dealing/scooping, so use it after hands-on sharing and grouping.
activities.intendedInsight: Both wordings — 'share among 3' and 'how many groups of 3' — are division, and a single division fact matches both a sharing picture and a grouping picture.
learnerActions: Read or hear short word problems and sort each into 'sharing' (share a total among a number of people/plates) or 'grouping' (make groups of a fixed size).
Match a division sentence like 12÷3=4 to BOTH a shared picture (3 plates with 4 each) and a grouped picture (4 groups of 3).
Fill in the answer to simple remainder-free division sentences, using counters to check.
activities.title: Sort the stories: sharing or grouping?

feedback: If a learner accepts the unequal shares, hand them the counters and have them redeal one-to-one, then count each friend's share.
Use fair-sharing language to connect to early fractions — sharing 1 cake between 2 is a half — keeping first examples exact with no remainder.
A talking partner cannot move the counters for the child, so make sure the child physically redistributes the quantity rather than only talking about it.
activities.intendedInsight: Talking through fairness reinforces that equal shares are the rule, while actually moving the counters is what lets the child make and check the equal shares.
learnerActions: A puppet or story character shares a set unfairly on purpose (gives one friend 'a lot'). Fix it so every friend gets an equal share.
Explain to the character why the new sharing is fair and the old one was not.
Pose and solve a fair-share dilemma aloud: 'We have 12 sweets and 4 friends — what's fair?' (3 each).
activities.title: Correct the unfair sharer
